title: Silent Degradation Detection and Automated Remediation Playbook
author: Asha Kapoor
content:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines how Redwood detects 'silent degradations' (performance or quality regressions that do not immediately trigger customer-facing errors) and how we automatically remediate or escalate them. It centralizes detection signals, automated mitigation actions, ownership, and customer communication templates.

Scope: Applies to hosted API, Dedicated, and Private tenants for production inference pipelines. Focus areas: inference quality drift (semantic regressions), behind-the-scenes latency/cost regressions, and resource contention that degrades tail latency without complete failures.

Principles

- Detect early using behavioral signals instead of waiting for incident thresholds.
- Prefer automated safe remediation (circuit breakers, model fallback, synthetic rollbacks) when available.
- Keep customers informed for any automated action that modifies their request routing, model variant, or cost profile.

Key Definitions

- Silent Degradation: Degradation in availability, latency tail, unit cost, or model output fidelity that does not meet an immediate SLA but will materially affect customer experience over time (e.g., 15% increase in 95th percentile latency sustained for 30 minutes while error rate remains <1%).
- Mitigation Ladder: Ordered set of remediation steps ranked by low customer-impact and safety-first (observability -> soft mitigation -> hard mitigation -> human escalation).
- Synthetic Journey: End-to-end customer request simulation that verifies correctness, latency, and token cost against a baseline.

Signals and Detection Rules

1) Telemetry signals (primary):
   - p95 latency increase: >20% over rolling 60-min baseline for a customer segment.
   - Median tokens-per-generation increase: >30% vs. expected prompt distribution.
   - Inference unit cost variance: >25% sustained for 30 minutes.
   - Model-quality drift: decrease in internal eval accuracy/QA score by >5% on control prompt-set.
   - Synthetic journey failure rate: >3% failed assertions in last 10 runs.

2) Composite alerts (trigger when 2+ signals occur within a 30-minute window):
   - Example: p95 latency + tokens increase -> composite degradation alert.

3) Noise control and suppression:
   - Require minimum sample size (50 requests) in 30-minute window to avoid noisy triggers.
   - Apply anomaly detection smoothing: use robust median-of-means to ignore one-off spikes.

Mitigation Ladder (Automated-first flow)

Stage 0 — Observability escalation (automatic, no customer impact):
- Enrich alert with correlating dimensions: region, model_variant, tenant_id, pod_id, request_path.
- Run synthetic journey (fast) against the same variant and region.
- Snapshot KV cache hit ratio and batch size distribution.
- Notify oncall via Slack channel #ops-customer-alerts with prefilled context.

Stage 1 — Soft mitigations (safe, reversible):
1. Adaptive single-tenant batching loosen: reduce max batch wait time from config (default 25 ms -> 10 ms) to reduce tail latency for latency-sensitive customers.
   - Command: curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/tenants/{tenant}/config -d '{"batch_wait_ms":10}'
2. Prefix-KV cache warmup disable/enable toggle: temporarily disable prefix cache prefetch for affected tenant to prevent thrash.
3. Reduce quantization aggressiveness for the specific model_variant (if supported) to restore tail latency at expense of small cost increase.
- Automation: playbook automation runs these incrementally with health checks after each change (10-minute stabilization window).

Stage 2 — Hard mitigations (automated but higher-impact):
1. Model-fallback to higher-latency but more stable variant (e.g., redwood-model-v2.small -> redwood-model-v2.base).
   - Route policy change: set "fallback=true" for affected tenant and route for 15 minutes.
2. Cross-region failover for regional capacity anomalies (only for customers with cross-region enabled).
3. Temporary request-throttling or per-tenant fairshare enforcement to protect shared capacity.
- Automation: require 3 confirmation checks (composite signal persists across 3 consecutive 10-minute windows) before applying.

Stage 3 — Human-in-the-loop and customer-impacting actions:
- Paging to SRE and Customer Success for coordinated action.
- Consider scheduled model rollback (if recent model rollout is correlated).
- Initiate coordinated customer communication and QBR action items.

Escalation matrix and Ownership

- Primary owner: SRE (eng-sre) — responsible for automated runbook maintenance and operations targeting.
- Secondary owner: Customer Success — responsible for customer notification and follow-up.
- Tertiary owner: Runtime/Serving team — responsible for fixing systemic regressions (kernel changes, batching logic).

Severity mapping (example):
- Sev-3 (Degradation): p95 latency up 20%, small customer impact. Action: Stages 0-1 automated. Notify CS.
- Sev-2 (Significant Degradation): p95 up 50% or synthetic failures >10%. Action: Stages 0-2 automated plus SRE paging.
- Sev-1 (Critical): sustained degradation causing customer SLA breach or data loss. Action: Full incident runbook; immediate human response and customer-wide comms.

Customer Communication Templates

- Auto-notify (low impact): "We detected increased latency affecting your tenant in region X. We've applied temporary mitigations and are monitoring. No action required on your side. Status: investigating."
- Escalated notification (when model-fallback or throttling applied): "To prevent downstream impact we temporarily routed requests to a stable model variant. Expected impact: small quality delta for 15–60 minutes. We will notify when normal routing is restored."

Implementation details and examples

1) Synthetic Journey definition (YAML example):
| name: conversational-check
| frequency_minutes: 5
| tenant_scope: control
| steps:
|   - send_prompt: "Summarize: The market yesterday..."
|   - assert_latency_lt_ms: 350
|   - assert_tokens_lt: 300
|   - compute_quality_score: baseline_eval.json

2) Example alert rule (pseudo):
- name: silent-degradation-composite
  condition: (p95_latency > 1.2 * rolling_p95) AND (median_tokens > 1.3 * rolling_median_tokens)
  min_samples: 50
  window: 30m
  action: trigger_auto_mitigation_workflow

3) Sample automation flow (CLI snippets):
- Run synthetic journey: 
  curl -X POST $SYNTH_API/run -d '{"journey":"conversational-check","region":"us-west-2"}'
- Apply batching config tweak: 
  curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/tenants/tenant-123/config -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"batch_wait_ms":10}'
- Apply model-fallback (atomic): 
  curl -X POST $ADMIN_API/routing -d '{"tenant":"tenant-123","route_override":{"model":"redwood-model-v2.base","duration_min":15}}'

Safety checks and guardrails

- Automatic changes must be bounded: no single automated change should increase tenant costs >20% without human approval.
- Any automated model-fallback that alters output fidelity requires CS notification and an opt-out flag for customers who have strict fidelity SLAs.
- All automated actions must be logged with request-level correlation IDs and rollback timers.

Testing and validation

- Nightly synthetic runs against Canary tenants to validate auto-remediation code paths.
- Game-day quarterly validation: simulate silent degrations (increase latency, reduce KV cache hits) and verify automation triggers and rollbacks.
- Regression validation in PRs that modify batching/kv/quantization code paths: include synthetic journey baseline runs in CI.

Runbook: Step-by-step response (when automation triggers)

1. T=0: Composite alert triggers -> run automated diagnostic snapshot (observability enrichment).
2. T=0–10m: Orchestrator runs synthetic journey and posts results to incident channel.
3. T=10–25m: Automation applies Stage 1 mitigations sequentially with 10-minute stabilize checks.
4. T=25–60m: If composite persists, automation promotes to Stage 2 mitigations; SRE is paged.
5. T>60m: If unresolved, escalate to incident playbook (oncall rotation, CS outreach, exec notification if >2 customers impacted).

Operational metrics to track

- Mean time to detect (MTTD) for silent degradations.
- % of degradations mitigated fully by automation (no human involvement).
- False positive rate of composite alerts.
- Average cost delta introduced by automated actions.
- Customer satisfaction delta post-remediation (tracked in QBR).

QBR inputs and Recommended Reporting

For Quarterly Business Reviews (CS + Customer): provide:
- Incidents summary that used this playbook (count, mitigation type, customer impact).
- MTTD/MTTR and how many were fully automated.
- Any recurring root causes and action items (e.g., batching kernel bug, KV cache cold-start).
- Cost vs. quality tradeoffs observed and recommended model/quantization profile changes.

Appendices

A. Sample JSON payload for alert enrichment:
{
  "alert_id":"sd-20260702-001",
  "tenant":"tenant-123",
  "signals":["p95_latency","tokens_increase"],
  "region":"us-west-2",
  "snapshot_time":"2026-07-02T14:35:00Z"
}

B. Quick checklist for Customer Success when notified:
1. Confirm automated action applied and duration.
2. Validate customer critical flows (support request or synthetic) if requested.
3. Proactively schedule a short postmortem if customer observes visible impact.
4. Log follow-up items in customer QBR agenda.

Document maintenance

- Owner: SRE (primary) — review every 3 months or after any major automation incident.
- Reviewer cadence: CS/Runtime/Observability teams to review changes prior to publication.
